title: The Von Neumann model, registers and buses

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The Von Neumann model and the stored program concept; the special purpose registers; the ALU, Control Unit and system clock; and how data is transferred between components on buses.

blocks.heading: The Von Neumann model and the stored program
blocks.text: Almost every computer follows one model, described by Von Neumann. The system has one memory that holds both the program's instructions and its data; a single processor that fetches, decodes and executes those instructions; and input, output and storage devices around them, connected by buses. The idea that carries the model is the stored program concept: a program's instructions are held in memory in the same way as its data, so the processor treats instructions as something to be fetched and obeyed, one after another, from memory. The consequence is generality. Because what the machine does is decided by the contents of its memory, the same hardware becomes a different machine whenever a different program is loaded: the office computer runs payroll in the morning, a game at lunch and a calculation in the afternoon, with nothing rewired, because the program is data that can be changed. Earlier machines were built wired to one task; the stored program is what ended that, and every piece of software in this course rests on it.

blocks.heading: The special purpose registers
blocks.text: Inside the CPU, a register is a small, very fast store, and the special purpose registers each have one fixed job. The Program Counter (PC) holds the memory address of the instruction that will be fetched next - not a count of instructions, but an address, which is why its value is copied to the MAR at every fetch. The Memory Address Register (MAR) holds the address of the location currently being read or written, and the Memory Data Register (MDR) holds the data or instruction travelling between the processor and memory: whatever is read arrives in the MDR, and whatever is written leaves from it. The Current Instruction Register (CIR) holds the instruction now being executed, after the fetch copies it there. The Accumulator (ACC) is where the ALU's working results are held: an addition's total lands in the accumulator, ready for the next operation to use it. The Index Register (IX) holds a base address that indexed addressing adds to, and the Status Register holds flags about the last operation - zero, negative, overflow - which later instructions can test. One further kind of register completes the picture: a general purpose register is one the program may use for its own working values, whereas a special purpose register has a role the program does not choose, so the difference is who decides what the register holds. A working habit for the register questions: name the register, then name its single fixed contents - the PC an address, the MAR an address, the MDR a travelling value, the CIR the instruction being executed, the ACC the ALU's running result - because the register's name is the answer to 'what does it hold', and each answer stays within its own kind of thing.

blocks.heading: ALU, Control Unit and system clock
blocks.text: Three parts of the processor do the work of executing. The Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU) computes: it performs the program's arithmetic and logic operations - addition, subtraction, comparisons - places the result in the accumulator, and sets the status flags that describe it. The Control Unit (CU) directs: an instruction sitting in the CIR says what must happen but does nothing by itself, and the control unit decodes it and sends the control signals that make the other components act, telling memory to read, registers to pass their contents, or the ALU to operate. Keep the boundary between the two straight: the control unit is one part of the CPU, not the whole of it - the ALU, the registers and the control unit are all parts, and the control unit's share is the decoding and the signalling. The system clock sets the pace: it generates regular timing pulses, and the CPU's steps proceed in step with those ticks, so a higher clock speed means more ticks per second and more instruction stages completed per second, which is why clock speed is one of the performance factors of the next unit.

blocks.heading: Buses: how the components talk
blocks.text: The components of the Von Neumann model are joined by three buses, and each bus carries one kind of thing. The address bus carries memory addresses: when the processor wants a location, the address travels on this bus. The data bus carries the actual data and instructions - the value read, the value written, the instruction fetched. The control bus carries control and timing signals, such as read and write, that tell each component what to do with what is on the other buses. Every memory access uses all three, in the same pattern: the address goes out on the address bus, a read or write signal goes out on the control bus, and the value travels on the data bus. The widths of the buses matter as much as their jobs. A wider address bus carries a larger address, so it can address more memory; a wider data bus moves more bits per transfer, so a 32-bit data bus moves 4 bytes in one transfer and a 64-bit bus 8. Both widths feed the performance story of the next unit, because they set how much the system can address and how much moves at once. A bus question to be ready for: which bus carries what? Answer by naming what travels - an address, a value, or a command - and the bus follows, because the three buses divide the traffic by kind and never share it.

blocks.heading: Worked example: one memory read, bus by bus
blocks.text: Trace the read of a value the processor needs, using every part of this unit. The processor places the address of the wanted location in the MAR. On the address bus, that address travels from the MAR to memory. On the control bus, a read signal travels with it, telling memory what to do. Memory finds the location and places its contents on the data bus, which carries the value back into the MDR. Now the value is inside the processor, ready to be used. Three buses, three jobs, and nothing travels on the wrong one: the address is an address, so it goes on the address bus; the read command is a signal, so it goes on the control bus; the value is data, so it comes home on the data bus. Test any described transfer the same way - name what travels, and the bus names itself.

blocks.heading: Common errors
blocks.text: Three slips recur here. Giving the program counter a counting job: the PC holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched, and the test is that its value is copied to the MAR at every fetch, because the MAR must hold an address. Describing the whole CPU when the control unit was asked for: the control unit decodes and signals, while the ALU computes and the registers hold - remove the ALU and the registers, and what is left is the CU's job. And putting data on the control bus: data and instructions travel on the data bus, addresses on the address bus, and signals such as read and write on the control bus, so the test is to name what travels.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The registers and buses here are the stage on which the Fetch-Execute cycle of 4.1.2 runs, and the same registers are addressed by the assembly language of 4.2. The gates of 3.2 are the ALU's building blocks, and the memory of 3.1 is what the buses reach.
